strengths: I think the paper is bringing out an important research question.

The general idea of expecting that LLMs can emulate code if we want to use them for more general software engineering tasks is an interesting one. I would encourage the authors to continue along this research direction.

The paper provides a very thorough investigation of LLMs' capability for code execution. They not only provide a reasonable framework to define strong or weak code execution capability but also have detailed error analysis. They also investigate more than 10 models across small to large, closed to open. This will be a valuable resource for readers interested in the capabilities of current LLMs.

It is interesting to study the "invalid reasoning path," which they define as incorrect intermediate output but correct end results or branch selection, etc. It shows how the model may not follow exactly how to execute the instructions for the current state, unlike a program, and then still get the final answer correct.

Many other insights are backed by results from many different models. For example, they also investigate the consistency of code execution ability across different test inputs that cover different paths and show that most LLMs are not consistent in the sense that while they can execute some test cases successfully, even with test cases going through the same path, they often may still get them wrong.
The paper is well-written and nicely structured. The figures and tables are well formatted and legible.
The story is engaging and the tackled topic interesting.
The proposed method promises improvements of previous work regarding the ability to pinpoint errors made by LLMs during reasoning at a lower inference cost.
This paper presents a novel framework, Code Execution Simulation (CES), to assess code reasoning in LLMs. Code execution capability is an important aspect to evaluate LLMs.
CES's design is diagnostic. By defining the notions of valid or invalid reasoning process, it can detect suspiciously correct output predictions under invalid reasoning.

CES uses a novel reasoning consistency metric to benchmark LLMs' code reasoning abilities as strong, weak and random, by executing multiple tests per program with same or different prime path coverage.
weaknesses: Overall I think the paper is not ready for publication yet.
The writing of the paper could be improved in places.
In Equation 1 the notation is not clear. CES and GT should have something to differentiate from the variables in the equation.
In Figure 7, the radar plot and legend are unclear.
The definition of prime paths being between any two program points requires justification.

RQ4 is the most important part of the paper. However, the results are underwhelming currently. The fact that there is no correlation between an LLM correctly emulating a piece of code and the LLM doing well on the programming task for that same piece of code does not support the hypothesis of the paper.
Emulating code is neither necessary nor sufficient to be able to find bugs; humans also find bugs by pattern matching based on experience.
The evaluation is limited to HumanEval and simple languages; the authors should explore programs outside of HumanEval and other programming languages such as C/C++ with more complex semantics.
It is not clear if the impact of variable values is discussed; for example, it isn't clear how large intermediate integers or long lists would affect the CSE results.

It is not clear why the proposed positions (branch taking, predicates, return value) are the most relevant positions; the exclusion of assignment statements is not justified and there is no evidence that the chosen set of statements sufficiently captures mispredictions.

The claim that predicting assignment values results in poor performance is not supported by experimental evidence; an ablation study comparing the chosen subset with a more comprehensive set including assignments is necessary.

The definition of invalid reasoning (marking reasoning as invalid when an intermediate state is incorrectly predicted but the consequence is predicted correctly) may not accurately capture whether the reasoning was indeed wrong, and lacks evidence that such cases always constitute incorrect reasoning.
Defining 'valid reasoning' to include instances where the model outputs an incorrect output is confusing.

The code evaluation may be unnatural and confusing to the model, artificially reducing performance, as suggested by many cases of 'suspiciously correct' outputs based on natural language reasoning that are inconsistent with the produced code reasoning.

Weak correlation of models in CES and other related program understanding tasks does not necessarily imply that models are subpar reasoners; it could imply that CES is not a format in which models can effectively express their code understanding.

Appendix A.6 shows stronger models perform well on bug localization, prediction, and repair, yet there is no correlation to CES, suggesting CES may not be the ideal format to elicit code reasoning in language models.
There is no control for the coverage of test cases on programs, which appears odd; a controlled experiment for different path coverage would be interesting.
Figure 7 is very difficult to parse, especially the legend, and the choice of chart format and grouping is unclear.
Figure 8 instruction reads 'You are given a piece of Python code and its _output_' while the model is clearly given _input_ below, which may be a typo with implications for the presented numbers.

The statement that 'LLMs with good performance in valid reasoning also make more invalid reasoning' seems contradictory because reasoning is either valid or invalid, and the sum should be constant; clarification is needed.

Using code execution simulation as a measure of a model’s code reasoning abilities is debatable because execution requires substantial computational accuracy, and it is unclear how computational skills relate to logical reasoning capabilities.

The definition of the 'invalid reasoning process' is ambiguous; in Equation 4, a compound property is considered 'invalid' when it contains both correct and incorrect predictions, but the example involving loop variable and loop iterable does not belong to the same property according to Section 3.1.
The authors found no correlation between CES and other coding tasks but did not analyze the reasons for this lack of correlation or consider other code comprehension tasks such as code summarization.

Several 'why' questions remain unanswered in the evaluation (e.g., why predictions differed from ground-truth values, why LLMs make suspiciously correct output predictions), and the authors relied solely on case analysis without providing quantitative data analysis.
